Access the LXD UI

  • The LXD web UI provides a graphical interface to manage LXD server and instances. You can access the UI using a TLS or a self-signed certificate, or use an external OIDC provider to sign in using Single Sign-On (SSO).

    For configuring the LXD web UI with a certificate, see How to access the LXD web UI.

    1. Expose LXD to the network by setting the core.https_address server configuration option, as shown in Core configuration: 
      lxc config set core.https_address :8443
    2. Access the UI in your browser by entering the server address. For example, https://192.168.105.41:8443.
    3. Set up the certificates that are required for the UI client to authenticate with the LXD server by following the steps in the UI.

      You have two options, depending on whether you already have a client certificate that is selected in the browser:

      1. If you do not have a certificate yet, click Create a new certificate. You are presented with instructions for creating a set of certificates, adding the public key to the server trust store, and adding the private key to your browser.
      2. If you already have a client certificate in your browser, select use an existing certificate to authorize the certificate with the server and reuse it.
    4. Refresh the browser and access the LXD UI.

    For logging in to the LXD UI using SSO, you must first configure LXD to authenticate using a preconfigured external OIDC provider. Once done, SSO options appear in the UI.

Attach the PowerFlex-based volume to a VM instance

  • After creating a custom storage volume, you can add it to one or more instances as a disk device. For more information, see How to manage storage volumes.

    Follow the below steps to attach the volume to a virtual machine instance.

    1. Log in to the LXD UI.
    2. Click Instances, and then select the virtual machine instance to which to attach the volume.
    3. Go to Configuration > Disk devices.
    4. Click Edit instance > Attach disk device.
    5. Choose a PowerFlex-based volume to attach, and then click Select.
    6. Click Save changes.
    7. Verify that the PowerFlex-based volume is attached to the virtual machine instance.
    8. Verify the attached PowerFlex volume from the operating system. 
      root@vm1:~# lsblk
      NAME    MAJ:MIN RM  SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS
      loop0     7:0    0 38.8M  1 loop /snap/snapd/21759
      loop1     7:1    0   64M  1 loop /snap/core20/2379
      loop2     7:2    0   87M  1 loop /snap/lxd/29351
      sda       8:0    0   10G  0 disk 
      ├─sda1    8:1    0  9.9G  0 part /
      ├─sda14   8:14   0    4M  0 part 
      └─sda15   8:15   0  106M  0 part /boot/efi
      sdb       8:16   0   64G  0 disk

Canonical LXD

  • Canonical LXD is a lightweight open source virtualization platform. An LXD cluster can support thousands of instances and can run system containers, VMs or both.

    Here are some of the benefits of LXD:

    • Scalable—LXD can be deployed as a single instance on a computer or across a large cluster of up to 50 members.
    • Secure—LXD provides unprivileged containers by default and VMs with modern virtual hardware, UEFI SecureBoot, as well as vTPM and AMD SEV as additional security options.
    • Lightweight—LXD is lightweight and can also run on platforms with limited resources.
    • Image-based—LXD supports images for many Linux distributions, including official Ubuntu images and community-provided images.
    • REST API—LXD is built around a REST API.

    Some of the LXD capabilities include:

    • Image-based workflow for launching VMs and containers. Integrated image server, with support for custom ISO images as well.
    • Web UI for easier deployment and management of your workloads.
    • Projects for multitenancy and workload organization.
    • Profiles for defining instance options, device and device options, cloud-init instructions and further instance customizations. Profiles can then easily be applied to any number of instances.
    • Various hardware passthrough options, including PCI, GPU, USB, block devices, NICs, disks.
    • Live VM migration, users can migrate running VMs between hosts with little or no downtime.
    • Backups, snapshots, and image transfer support.
    • High availability through clustering with Ceph and OVN for distributed storage and networking. All these options are combined in the Canonical document What is a MicroCloud?.
    • Various storage backend options, including directory, BTRFS, LVM, ZFS, Ceph, and Dell PowerFlex.
    • Various networking options, including bridge and OVN for fully controlled networks as well as physical, SR-IOV, and Macvlan support for external network types.
    • Third-party integrations with tools like Terraform and Ansible are available. Custom integrations are possible through the LXD REST API.

Conclusion

  • Canonical LXD is an open source virtualization platform that can be configured and deployed on Dell PowerFlex infrastructure. The LXD UI is natively integrated with Dell PowerFlex storage and offers the capability to view storage info and perform storage operations directly from the UI. The performance test results described in this paper demonstrate that PowerFlex with Canonical LXD can achieve high performance at sub millisecond latencies. Virtual machines and system containers can be configured with attached PowerFlex storage while providing a secure and scalable environment with minimal overhead.

Configure an LXD cluster

  • This section details the steps for creating an LXD cluster using three compute nodes. When forming an LXD cluster, you start with a bootstrap server. This bootstrap server can be an existing LXD server or a newly installed one. After that, other LXD servers can join to the cluster using a token created by the initial node.

    For more information about forming a cluster, see How to form a cluster.

    • Initialize the bootstrap server
    • Join additional servers

  • Join additional servers

    Note: The servers that you add should be newly installed LXD servers. If you are using existing servers, clear their contents before joining them because any existing data will be lost.

    1. Request to join an existing cluster: 
      sudo lxd init
    2. Authenticate with the cluster.

Create a PowerFlex storage pool

  • The LXD UI is natively integrated with Dell PowerFlex storage and offers the capability to view storage information and perform storage operations directly from the UI. This section details the steps for creating the PowerFlex storage pool in the LXD UI. For more information about creating a PowerFlex storage pool, see PowerFlex storage in LXD.

    1. Log in to the LXD UI.
    2. Click Storage > Create pool.
    3. Enter the following pool information:
      • Name
      • Select Dell PowerFlex as the Driver.
      • PowerFlex pool
      • Domain
      • Gateway
      • Username
      • Password
    4. Verify the corresponding YAML configuration file.
    5. Click Create.
    6. Verify that the PowerFlex storage pool is created.

Create a PowerFlex storage volume

  • This procedure details the steps for how to create, configure, view, and resize PowerFlex volumes in LXD. For more information, see PowerFlex volume in LXD.

    1. Log in to the LXD UI.
    2. Click Storage > Volumes > Create volume.
    3. Select a storage pool as the PowerFlex storage pool.

      For example, powerflex-storage.

    4. Enter the name and size of the volume.
    5. Select the content type block.
    6. Click Create.
    7. Notice that the volume pfx-vol1 is available in the Volumes tab.
    8. To resize the volume, click the volume that was created.
    9. Click Configuration > Edit volume.
    10. Change the volume size and click Save changes.

Create a VM instance

  • In an LXD cluster, each instance resides on one of the cluster members. You can operate each instance from any cluster member. You do not have to log in to the cluster member on which the instance is located.

    For more information, see How to create instances.

    Follow the below steps to create virtual machine instances.

    1. Log in to the LXD UI.
    2. Click Instances > Create instance.
    3. On the resulting screen, optionally enter a name and description for the instance.
    4. Click Browse images to select the image to be used for the instance.
    5. To further modify the instance configuration or add devices to the instance, go to any of the tabs under Advanced.
    6. You can also edit the full instance configuration on the YAML configuration tab.
    7. Finally, click either Create or Create and start to create the instance.

Executive summary

  • Enterprises today are looking for solutions to manage their virtual environments in a secure and cost-effective way. Canonical LXD is a modern, secure, and powerful open source virtualization platform. LXD supports images for many Linux distributions and is built around a powerful, yet simple, REST API. LXD scales from one instance on a single machine to a cluster, enabling you to run development and production workloads.

    LXD allows you to easily set up a system that feels like a small private cloud. You can run workloads in an efficient way while keeping your resources optimized. LXD is a strong choice for running and managing virtual machines and infrastructure in a cost-effective manner.

    PowerFlex is a software-defined infrastructure that is designed to reduce operational and infrastructure complexity. It empowers organizations to move faster by delivering flexibility, elasticity, and simplicity with predictable performance and resiliency at scale. The PowerFlex family provides a foundation that combines compute and high-performance storage resources in a managed, unified fabric. With the capabilities available as part of the PowerFlex platform, administrators can easily implement a scalable, high performance, and flexible solution that is designed for the modern data center.

    This white paper describes the deployment and configuration of Canonical LXD cluster on Dell PowerFlex infrastructure to create, manage, and monitor virtual machine instances. This white paper also covers the evaluation of basic performance tests on virtual machines.

Install LXD

  • This procedure details the steps for installing the LXD on a compute node. The easiest way to install LXD is to install the snap package. For more information about installing LXD, see the Ubuntu document How to install LXD.

    1. Connect to the first compute node using SSH.
    2. Install snapd:
      1. Run snap version to find out if snap is installed on your system: 
        root@co-node1:~# snap version
        snap    2.63+22.04ubuntu0.1
        snapd   2.63+22.04ubuntu0.1
        series  16
        ubuntu  22.04
        kernel  5.15.0-122-generic
      2. If not installed, then install snapd using the following command: 
        sudo apt update
        sudo apt install snapd
    3. Enter the following command to install LXD. In the example below, the 5.21 LTS release is installed. 
      sudo snap install lxd --channel=5.21/stable
      Note: If LXD is already installed and must be updated to the latest LTS version, run the following command: 
      sudo snap refresh lxd --channel=5.21/stable


    4. Check if the current user is part of the lxd group (the group was automatically created during the previous step): 
      getent group lxd | grep "$USER"
      1. If this command returns a result, you are set up correctly and can go to the next step.
      2. If there is no result, enter the following commands to add the current user to the lxd group (which is required to grant the user permission to interact with LXD): 
        sudo usermod -aG lxd "$USER"
        newgrp lxd
    5. Repeat Step 1 to Step 4 on the other compute nodes to install LXD on them.

Install the PowerFlex SDC Driver

  • The following requirements must be met before installing the PowerFlex SDC driver on all compute nodes:

    • Obtain the PowerFlex SDC driver installation files for the Ubuntu operating system.
    • Note the virtual IP address or MDM IP address of the PowerFlex storage cluster.

    This procedure details the steps for installing the PowerFlex SDC driver on all compute nodes for connecting to the PowerFlex storage.

    1. Log in to the first compute node running the Ubuntu operating system using SSH.
    2. Upload the PowerFlex SDC driver installation file for the Ubuntu operating system into the LXD compute node.
    3. Install the PowerFlex SDC driver from the command line: 
      MDM_IP=192.168.151.50,192.168.152.50 dpkg -i EMC-ScaleIO-sdc-4.5-0.287.Ubuntu.22.04.x86_64.deb
    4. Verify that the PowerFlex SDC driver is installed using the following command: 
      root@co-node1:/home/user# systemctl status scini.service
      ● scini.service - LSB: This script is responsible to control the scini service.
           Loaded: loaded (/etc/init.d/scini; generated)
           Active: active (exited) since Mon 2024-10-07 09:07:47 UTC; 1 week 2 days ago
             Docs: man:systemd-sysv-generator(8)
              CPU: 341ms
      Oct 07 09:07:47 co-node1 scini[2016]: scinia is not ready yet...
      Oct 07 09:07:47 co-node1 scini[2016]: Success configuring module
      Oct 07 09:07:47 co-node1 scini[2016]:  *
      Oct 07 09:07:47 co-node1 systemd[1]: Started LSB: This script is responsible to control the scini service..
    5. Repeat step 1 to step 4 to install the PowerFlex SDC driver on the other compute nodes.

      For more information about PowerFlex SDC installation, see the Dell PowerFlex 4.5.x. Install and Upgrade Guide.

Logical architecture

  • The following diagram shows the logical architecture of this solution.

    The PowerFlex cluster is deployed in a two-layer architecture on four PowerFlex storage-only nodes using PowerFlex Manager. The four storage-only nodes are installed with the PowerFlex embedded operating system. The three compute nodes are configured as an LXD cluster running the Ubuntu operating system.

    The user can install the SDC manually on compute only nodes. After volumes are configured, the user can map them from the PowerFlex storage pool to the LXD compute node. LXD can use that storage through the LXD UI. The user manually controls the life cycle of the SDC on LXD compute nodes.

    For more information about the hardware and software versions that are used in this solution, see Test configuration.

Network architecture

  • The following diagram shows the network architecture of this solution.

    At the physical layer, two Top of Rack (TOR) switches are used for redundancy and load-balancing purposes. A peer link is configured on both the TOR switches. VLANs are created to separate different traffic types on the network bonds.

    The following table shows the different networks that are configured for this solution. For more information, see PowerFlex node VLAN setup.

    Table 3. Network details
    Network type VLAN ID
    Operating System (OS) Management 105
    PowerFlex Management 150
    PowerFlex Data 1 151
    PowerFlex Data 2 152
    Note: The Operating System Management network must be routable to the PowerFlex Management network to access the PowerFlex cluster.

Overview

  • This section describes the basic performance tests that are performed using the FIO tool.

    FIO is an open-source tool that is used for testing I/O performance. It enables different types of I/O workloads, from sequential reads to random writes, and a mixture of random reads/writes according to user-defined settings. In this paper, the PowerFlex team has evaluated 100 percent random read and mixed (50 percent read/write) FIO workloads on Canonical LXD VMs attached with PowerFlex volumes.

    The following metrics are used to measure the performance:

    • IOPS: Read/write IOs per second.
    • Throughput: Read/written data rate per second, in MB/s.
    • Latency: Time for each I/O operation.

  • PowerFlex in the public cloud

    PowerFlex software storage services can be deployed on recommended instances (with attached storage) in Amazon Web Services or Microsoft Azure. Only the MG data layout and Independent (disaggregated) architecture is supported. Fault Sets may be used to distribute the cluster across multiple Availability Zones, improving resiliency even during AZ disruptions. Native asynchronous replication may be used to migrate data between cloud and on-premises PowerFlex systems, or to establish cloud-based BC/DR data protection schemes.

PowerFlex consumption options

  • PowerFlex CSI/CSM

    An important component outside of PowerFlex that enables a flexible consumption model for Kubernetes is the PowerFlex CSI driver, developed as a part of the Dell Kubernetes strategy. After loading the CSI driver for PowerFlex into Kubernetes, it can be used to provision persistent volumes from the underlying PowerFlex storage resource. If the Kubernetes deployment is running low on PowerFlex storage resources, you can add PowerFlex storage nodes to increase the system capacity and performance.

    The CSI driver connects the PowerFlex system and Kubernetes deployments. It is a storage broker which dynamically provisions volumes from PowerFlex through the PowerFlex API gateway to the Kubernetes cluster. Once the volume is available on PowerFlex, it is immediately mapped to the requesting pod. If a pod is destroyed or rescheduled, the CSI plug-in ensures that the volumes are remapped upon rescheduling of that pod.

    • Customers running Kubernetes clusters on PowerFlex use the Dell Container Storage Modules (CSM), which extend the CSI driver capabilities. These modules:
    • Provide enterprise storage capabilities to Kubernetes for cloud-native stateful applications.
    • Reduce management complexity, so that developers can independently use enterprise storage with ease and automate daily operations.
    • Extends storage functionality and capabilities beyond using the CSI driver alone.

    These modules include snapshot, observability, authorization, application mobility, and resiliency. PowerFlex supports multiple operating systems, PowerFlex is validated with the leading Kubernetes distributions as shown in PowerFlex for different Kubernetes distributions.

PowerFlex deployment architectures

  • Independent architecture

    In an independent architecture, or disaggregated architecture, some nodes provide storage capacity for data in applications, while other separate and independent nodes provide compute resources for applications and workloads. Compute and storage resources can be scaled independently by adding nodes to the cluster while it remains active. This separation of compute and storage resources helps to minimize software licensing costs in certain situations. This architecture can be ideal for high-performance databases and application workloads.

    Disaggregation gives organizations the freedom to choose different LCM options that best align with their operational models. Not only can PowerFlex Manager manage the LCM of the PowerFlex storage infrastructure, but it can also manage LCM of PowerFlex compute nodes. With this freedom there is also the choice to manage compute estates that connect to PowerFlex with other tools. For example, VxRail Dynamic Nodes connected to PowerFlex using VxRail Manager automation.

PowerFlex family

  • PowerFlex software-defined infrastructure enables broad consolidation across the data center, encompassing most workloads. The software-first architecture enables automation and programmability of the complete infrastructure stack. PowerFlex provides scalability, performance, and resiliency to enable effortless adherence to stringent workload SLAs

    The PowerFlex family provides a foundation that combines compute and high-performance storage resources in a managed unified fabric. PowerFlex comes in flexible consumption options (rack, appliance, custom nodes, or in the public cloud) that enable independent (disaggregated) architectures. PowerFlex is ideal for high-performance applications and databases, building an agile private/hybrid cloud, or consolidating resources in heterogeneous environments.

Prerequisites

  • The following requirements must be met before installing the LXD on a compute node:

    • The PowerFlex SDC driver must be installed, and compute nodes must be added to PowerFlex as mentioned in Installing the PowerFlex SDC driver on a compute node.
    • Ensure that at least 20 GiB of free disk space exists before starting with installation.
